description: An independent team of Pakistani teenagers with experience in robotics competitions, hackathons and exhibitions. We’re using NASA Earth data on soil moisture, rainfall, heat and groundwater to help farmers explore crop rotations that conserve water, strengthen soil and build long-term resilience.
summary: Kisan AI is a farm decision-support web app that helps farmers choose crop rotations that save water, protect soil and cope with a changing climate. For the farmer’s district, it combines 20 years of NASA POWER climate with NASA satellite readings: SMAP soil moisture, GPM IMERG rain, MODIS greenness and heat, GRACE water storage and SRTM slope. It then compares the farmer’s current rotation with the three best alternatives, scored on water, soil health, weather safety, income and fodder. For each option it shows why it was suggested, the evidence, the risks to check locally and what the data cannot tell, in Urdu, Punjabi or English, by text or voice. This matters because rising heat, falling groundwater and tired soil threaten millions of small farms in Pakistan, where most fields repeat the same thirsty crops every year. Kisan AI turns NASA data into a decision a farmer can act on, while the final choice stays with the farmer.
details:
What it does & how it works
Kisan AI compares a farmer’s current crop rotation with the three best alternatives for their district, and explains the choice in plain Urdu, Punjabi or English. The farmer enters their location, land, water source, crops and goals. Kisan AI then gathers:

  • 20 years of daily NASA POWER climate: rainfall, heat days above 40 °C, frost nights, heavy-rain days and their trends.
  • NASA satellite readings at the district’s location point: SMAP root-zone soil moisture, GPM IMERG rainfall, MODIS greenness (NDVI), ground temperature and land cover, and GRACE/GRACE-FO water storage. These are read pixel by pixel from NASA GIBS by converting each map color back into its physical value.
  • NASA SRTM 30 m elevation, which gives the slope and erosion hotspots around that point.
  • Government soil surveys: USDA SSURGO for US farms, and the Soil Survey of Pakistan and WAPDA for Pakistan.

Each rotation is scored 0-100 on water, soil health, weather safety, income and fodder, weighted by the farmer’s own priorities. A second, statistical method replays each of the last 20 years of NASA weather through every rotation, so rotations that fail in hot or dry years rank lower. Both rankings are shown side by side.

Benefits

  • For every rotation, the app shows why it was suggested, the NASA evidence, the benefits, the risks to check locally, and what we don’t know.
  • A 12-month field calendar marks bare-field months and shows irrigation need in mm per year.
  • What-if sliders test a hotter (up to +3 °C) or drier (down to -40% rain) future.
  • A NASA layer map shows soil moisture, rain, ground heat, vegetation, Landsat field-scale imagery and erosion hotspots.
  • A farming-only AI assistant answers questions from the farm’s own NASA and soil data, by text or voice.

Intended impact
Pakistan’s farms face rising heat, falling groundwater and tired soil, and most repeat thirsty rotations like wheat-rice every year. Moving even part of that land to rotations with a legume or a less thirsty crop saves groundwater, rebuilds soil nitrogen and spreads climate risk. Kisan AI is built for small farmers and the extension workers who advise them. It runs on free, open data, so it can reach millions of farms at no data cost, and because it already works for both Pakistan and the United States, the method can extend to other regions.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: JavaScript (React/JSX), HTML and CSS
  • Web app: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet (maps), Recharts (charts)
  • Back end: Node.js serverless functions, hosted on Vercel
  • Data: NASA POWER API, NASA GIBS, SRTM via OpenTopoData, USDA Soil Data Access, Open-Meteo
  • AI: Claude Code (Anthropic) to write the program for the website, under the team’s direction; Google Gemini for the assistant, speech-to-text and spoken Urdu (the rotation scores are rule-based, not AI)
  • Hardware: none needed. It runs in the browser of any phone or computer.

What makes it creative

  • It reads real numbers out of NASA’s map images using GIBS colour tables.
  • It compares a transparent rule-based score with a 20-year statistical replay.
  • It separates orchards from field crops by combining MODIS land cover with a year of NDVI.
  • It builds a “What we don’t know” section into every recommendation.

Factors we considered

  • Farmers’ realities: small plots, the machines they own or can hire, where they sell, fodder for animals, and canal, tube-well or rain-fed water.
  • Language and literacy: Urdu, Punjabi and English, a right-to-left layout, and voice for farmers who cannot read.
  • Data limits, stated openly: readings are taken at the district’s center point, not at each field; satellite pixels are larger than most fields, GRACE measures total water storage, not groundwater alone, and there are no field yield records yet, so we did not train a machine-learning model.
  • Decision support, not decision making: the final choice stays with the farmer, and the app says to check locally.
